question: Why does this project's handshake use a simplified Noise 'IK'-style two-message exchange instead of porting WireGuard's real wire format byte-for-byte?
answer_hinglish:
Decision PLAN.md mein clearly likha hai: yeh project WireGuard ka exact byte-format copy nahi karta, balki uska core shape rakhta hai -- mutual authentication aur forward secrecy, jo ECDH algebra se directly fall out hote hain. Jo chhoda gaya hai woh OPERATIONAL hardening hai: WireGuard ka real handshake ek timestamp bhi fold karta hai (handshake-replay protection ke liye) aur ek cookie/MAC mechanism (DoS resistance ke liye, taaki fake handshake flood se CPU na khaye).

Stage 1 ka point yeh samajhna hai ki ek VPN tunnel ACTUALLY kaise authenticate karta hai, operational edge cases nahi. Agar main timestamp aur cookie bhi add karta, toh core teaching point (DH algebra se authentication 'for free' aana) dilute ho jaata extra bookkeeping ke beech.

Trade-off honest hai: is design mein ek captured HANDSHAKE_INIT replay ho sakta hai (harmless extra attempt banata hai, koi working session nahi), aur koi rate-limit nahi hai repeated attempts ke against -- README ke 'Known and NOT handled' mein yeh explicitly documented hai. Production VPN banane se pehle yeh dono add karna zaroori hoga.
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate essential cryptographic shape (authentication + forward secrecy) aur operational hardening (DoS resistance, replay protection) ke beech distinction samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek car ka working engine prototype banana jo drive karta hai, versus ek production car jisme crumple zones, airbags, aur anti-theft alarm bhi hon -- dono 'car' hain, par ek teaching prototype hai aur doosra deployable product.
how_it_works: Message 1: initiator apna ephemeral public key aur (encrypted) static public key bhejta hai. Message 2: responder apna ephemeral public key aur ek empty-payload confirmation bhejta hai, teen chained DH terms se derive ki gayi key se encrypted.
in_this_project: src/handshake.ts ka header comment aur PLAN.md ka 'Decisions' section dono isi trade-off ko explain karte hain -- buildHandshakeInit aur buildHandshakeResponse hi poora do-message exchange hain, koi timestamp ya cookie field wire.ts ke message layouts mein nahi hai.
advantages: Core authentication/forward-secrecy mechanism stays easy to reason about and test
Fewer moving parts to get wrong while learning the ECDH algebra
Honestly documented gap instead of a silent, unexplained omission
disadvantages: A captured HANDSHAKE_INIT can be replayed to force harmless but repeated handshake attempts
No DoS-resistance cookie means a flood of fake inits can burn CPU on ECDH computations
Not a drop-in replacement for real WireGuard -- not interoperable with it
common_mistakes: Assuming this handshake is wire-compatible with real WireGuard
Thinking the missing cookie/timestamp is a bug rather than a documented scope decision
Believing authentication is weaker because it is 'simplified' -- the DH algebra guarantee is unchanged
follow_up_questions: What exact bytes would you add to support a handshake-replay-protection timestamp?
How would a cookie/MAC mechanism change the responder's receiveHandshakeInit flow?
Why doesn't dropping the timestamp/cookie weaken the mutual-authentication guarantee itself?

question: Why does AntiReplayWindow use a fixed-size sliding bitmap instead of a growing set of seen counters?
answer_hinglish:
Fixed-size bitmap chuna gaya hai kyunki yeh BOUNDED memory deta hai aur O(1) accept/reject, chahe session kitne bhi packets carry kare -- exactly wahi structure jo real WireGuard (RFC 6479-style) use karta hai. Ek growing `Set<number>` ke saath, memory session ki lifetime mein unboundedly badhti jaati, kyunki har naya counter set mein add hota rehta.

Bitmap ka trade-off yeh hai: `size` bits (default 2048) se zyada purana koi counter automatically 'forgotten' ho jaata hai -- woh ab TOO_OLD maana jaata hai, chahe woh genuinely replay ho ya nahi. Ek set ke saath, theoretically HAR counter yaad reh sakta hai forever, par is cost par ki memory kabhi free nahi hoti.

Project mein `AntiReplayWindow` constructor mein `size` bits allocate karta hai (`size / 8` bytes ka Uint8Array), aur `slot(counter) = counter % size` se bit-index nikalta hai -- yeh modulo wraparound hi bitmap ko 'sliding' banata hai: purane counters ka bit naturally reuse ho jaata hai jab window aage slide karti hai (`record()` mein `clear()` loop). Yeh 2048-size default itna generous hai ki koi bhi realistic out-of-order delay cover ho jaaye, bina memory ko unbounded chhode.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate bounded-memory data structures ka trade-off samajhta hai security-correctness ke against, aur WireGuard ki actual design choice ko reason kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek security guard ek fixed-size notebook mein last 2048 visitor IDs likhta hai, purane naturally overwrite ho jaate hain -- infinite notebook rakhne se better hai ek chhota, predictable-size notebook jo kabhi full nahi hota.
how_it_works: bitmap = new Uint8Array(size / 8); slot(counter) = counter % size; record() slides `highest` forward and clears every slot that newly enters the window before setting the new counter's bit.
in_this_project: src/replay-window.ts ka AntiReplayWindow class -- constructor size validate karta hai (positive multiple of 8), record() ka slide-and-clear loop O(size) bounded hai even if counter jumps far ahead.
advantages: Fixed, predictable memory footprint regardless of session traffic volume
O(1) check/record cost, no growing collection to search or garbage-collect
Matches the structure real WireGuard uses, so the lesson transfers directly
disadvantages: A packet delayed by more than `size` counters is rejected as TOO_OLD even if it was never replayed
Window size choice is a tuning knob -- too small rejects legitimate reordering, too large wastes memory
Unlike a set, the bitmap cannot answer 'has this counter EVER been seen' beyond the current window
common_mistakes: Using an unbounded Set and assuming memory growth is fine for a long-lived session
Picking a window size without considering real network reordering/jitter characteristics
Forgetting that slots repeat every `size` counters, so stale bits must be cleared on slide
follow_up_questions: What real-world factor should drive the choice of window size (2048 here)?
What happens correctness-wise if the window size were set to 8 instead of 2048?
How would you test that sliding the window doesn't leave stale bits from an evicted counter?

question: Why does every transport packet carry a receiver-chosen id instead of the sender's identity or socket address?
answer_hinglish:
Receiver-chosen id (`myReceiverId`/`peerReceiverId`) use hota hai kyunki decrypt karne ke liye sirf ek MAP LOOKUP chahiye, scan ya 'yeh address se aaya hai toh yeh peer hoga' wala assumption nahi. Yeh mirrors karta hai WireGuard ka real receiver index design.

Alternative design hota sender ki identity (jaise peer name) ya socket address ko packet mein daalna. Dono problematic hain: identity ek plaintext field hoti jo har packet mein repeat hoti (kuch extra metadata leak), aur socket address NAT/roaming ke scenario mein change ho sakta hai -- isliye address-based lookup fragile hota.

Project mein yeh id handshake ke time assign hota hai: Session constructor mein `myReceiverId` woh value hai jo DOOSRI side ko stamp karna hai packets par jo IS side ko address kiye jaate hain, aur `peerReceiverId` woh hai jo yeh side stamp karega packets jo DOOSRI side ko jaate hain -- receiver, sender nahi, apna lookup key choose karta hai. `Peer.sessionsByReceiverId` map se `decryptPacket` seedha O(1) session nikal leta hai, bina kisi scan ke. Yeh design NAT/roaming ke liye future-proof hai, chahe stage 1 ko khud iski zaroorat nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer samajhna chahta hai ki candidate dispatch-by-lookup-key ka design pattern samajhta hai aur yeh bhi ki yeh pattern NAT/roaming jaise future requirements ko kaise aasan banata hai.
real_world_analogy: Courier company tumhe EK tracking number deti hai jab tum package bhejte ho -- woh number receiver ke system mein lookup karta hai, chahe sender ka address ya naam kuch bhi badal jaaye beech mein.
how_it_works: During the handshake, each side generates its own receiver id and hands it to the other. Every outbound transport packet is stamped with the PEER's receiver id; the receiving side demultiplexes by looking that id up in `sessionsByReceiverId`.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts ka sessionsByReceiverId map aur installSession method; src/session.ts ke myReceiverId/peerReceiverId constructor params. Session.encrypt() stamps the PEER's receiverId, not this side's identity.
advantages: Decrypting an inbound packet is a single map lookup, never a scan or linear search
No dependency on which socket address a packet arrived from
Naturally supports future NAT traversal / endpoint roaming without a wire format change
disadvantages: An extra 4 bytes per packet versus assuming the socket address identifies the sender
Receiver ids must be managed/reused carefully if a session is ever torn down and rebuilt
Requires the handshake to successfully exchange ids before any transport traffic is possible
common_mistakes: Confusing the receiver id with the sender's identity -- it is chosen by whoever will RECEIVE future packets
Assuming the socket address a packet arrived from determines which session handles it
Reusing a receiver id across sessions without checking for collisions
follow_up_questions: If a peer's IP address changes mid-session (roaming), why does this id-based design make that easier to handle?
What happens if two different sessions ended up with the same receiver id by coincidence?
Why is the receiver id assigned during the handshake rather than negotiated afterward?

question: Why does this VPN carry opaque byte payloads instead of parsing and routing real IP packets?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh explicitly by-design hai, project brief ke mutaabik -- README aur PLAN.md dono ka 'Not in scope' section isko directly bolta hai. Is project ka point VPN TUNNELING ka core idea samajhna hai (ECDH handshake, AEAD transport, anti-replay), IP routing ek alag, bada topic hai jiski is stage ko zaroorat nahi.

Agar real IP packets carry karte, toh extra complexity aa jaati: IP header parsing, ek routing table maintain karna (kaunsa destination IP kis tunnel se jaata hai), aur host ke actual network stack se interaction (jo root/admin privileges chahta, jo yeh environment nahi deta). Yeh sab TunDevice ke scope se bahar hai -- TunDevice.send()/onReceive() sirf `Buffer` leta/deta hai, koi IP semantics nahi janta.

Src code mein dekho: `tun.send(Buffer.from("hello, bob"))` -- yeh koi IP packet nahi hai, bas raw application bytes hain. Engine (VpnNode) unhe encrypt/decrypt karta hai, kabhi unka content interpret nahi karta. Yeh choice test karna aasan banata hai: demo.ts mein bhi simple text strings use hote hain, kisi IP stack simulation ki zaroorat nahi padti.
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate scope boundaries samajhta hai aur honestly bol sakta hai ki kya feature NAHI hai, bina overclaiming kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier company sirf sealed boxes transport karti hai, box ke andar kya hai (chitthi, parcel, ya kuch bhi) usse interpret nahi karti -- VPN tunnel bhi yahi karta hai, bytes carry karta hai, unka meaning nahi janta.
how_it_works: TunDevice.send(packet: Buffer) hands an opaque byte buffer to the engine; VpnNode encrypts and ships it over UDP, the other side decrypts and calls deliver() with the same raw bytes, untouched.
in_this_project: src/tun.ts ka TunDevice interface aur InMemoryTunDevice -- dono sirf Buffer type use karte hain. src/demo.ts mein Buffer.from("hello, bob") jaisa plain text payload hi test data hai, koi IP header kahin nahi hai.
advantages: Keeps the project focused on handshake/AEAD/anti-replay, not IP routing
No need for root/admin privileges or a real kernel network stack
Simple to test with plain strings instead of constructing real IP packets
disadvantages: Cannot actually carry real network traffic the way a production VPN client does
No routing table, so it cannot decide which tunnel a given destination IP should use
Never exercises any IP-header-parsing edge cases a real VPN would face
common_mistakes: Assuming this project could be pointed at real network traffic without major additions
Confusing the opaque-payload design with a limitation of the crypto layer (it is a scope choice, not a crypto one)
Thinking TunDevice needs to understand packet contents to do its job
follow_up_questions: What would need to change in TunDevice/VpnNode to carry real IP packets?
Why does this design need no routing table today, and when would it need one?
What privilege requirement would adding real IP packet support introduce?

question: Why does AntiReplayWindow expose two separate methods, check() and record(), instead of one combined checkAndRecord()?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh split is project ka SABSE important design decision hai anti-replay ke liye. check() PURE hai (no mutation) aur record() mutate karta hai -- do alag methods isliye hain taaki Session.decrypt() check-BEFORE-decrypting aur record-ONLY-AFTER-authenticating kar sake, bina ek doosre ka side effect chhupaye.

Agar combined `checkAndRecord()` hota, toh caller ko yeh choice nahi milti ki record kab ho -- woh decrypt se pehle ya baad, dono scenario mein IMPLICITLY ek hi call mein ho jaata. Problem yeh hai: agar record check ke saath hi ho jaaye (decrypt se pehle), toh ek FORGED packet (jiska tag abhi verify hua hi nahi) ek guessed counter ko 'seen' mark kar sakta hai -- real sender ka BAAD mein aane wala genuine packet us counter ke saath wrongly REPLAY reject ho jaayega. Yeh exact gap README's mutation S2 mein document hai: 'a counter recorded as seen BEFORE its tag verifies'.

Session.decrypt() mein order dekho: pehle `window.check(counter)` (cheap rejection, AEAD decrypt se pehle), phir AEAD decrypt try karo, aur SIRF success par `window.record(counter)` call hota hai. Combined method yeh ordering flexibility chhin leta -- separate methods hi is correctness-critical sequencing ko possible banate hain.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki ek API split (vs combine) kabhi sirf style choice nahi, balki correctness-critical ordering ko enable karne ke liye hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek bank teller pehle cheque ki signature verify karta hai, SIRF verify hone ke baad hi account balance update karta hai -- agar balance pehle update ho jaaye signature check se pehle, ek forged cheque bhi paisa nikaal sakta hai.
how_it_works: check(counter) returns ACCEPT/REPLAY/TOO_OLD without touching the bitmap. record(counter) mutates the bitmap and slides `highest` forward. Session.decrypt() calls check() first, attempts AEAD decrypt, and only calls record() after decrypt succeeds.
in_this_project: src/replay-window.ts mein check() aur record() do alag public methods hain; src/session.ts ke decrypt() method mein exact ordering: check -> try aeadDecrypt -> record ONLY on success.
advantages: Enables the correctness-critical check-before-decrypt, record-after-authenticate ordering
check() being pure makes it trivially unit-testable without mutating shared state
Separating concerns makes the one hard invariant (never record an unauthenticated counter) visible in one place
disadvantages: Two method calls instead of one -- a caller could mistakenly call record() without calling check() first
Slightly more API surface to document and get right than a single combined call
Relies on caller discipline (Session.decrypt) to use both methods in the correct order
common_mistakes: Writing a combined checkAndRecord() that always records regardless of whether decryption later succeeds
Calling record() before the AEAD tag has actually verified (mutation S2's exact bug)
Assuming check() is safe to skip since record() alone 'also knows' the counter
follow_up_questions: What observable bug would recording before authenticating actually cause, step by step?
Why is check() specifically designed to never mutate state?
How would you test that record() is never reached when the AEAD tag fails?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Split API thoda zyada discipline maangta hai callers se (dono methods sahi order mein call karna), par yeh discipline sirf EK jagah (Session.decrypt) enforce karni padti hai, aur woh jagah already is project ka most-tested path hai. Combined method 'safer-looking' lagta, par actually ek IMPLICIT ordering choice chhupa deta jo galat bhi ho sakti thi.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi future caller directly record() call kare bina check() ke, ya decrypt se pehle hi record kare, toh attacker ek guessed counter wala forged packet bhej ke real sender ka future legitimate packet permanently block kara sakta hai -- isi gap ko mutation S2 ne real tareeke se reveal kiya tha.
advanced.alternatives: Ek combined checkAndRecord(counter, verifyFn) jo verification callback leta aur internally order enforce karta -- yeh possible hai par extra indirection introduce karta hai aur AEAD call ko replay-window module ke andar leak kar deta, jo abhi clean separation hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Behavior scale-independent hai -- yeh ek per-packet correctness concern hai, throughput ya session count se nahi badalta. 100x sessions par bhi har Session apna independent AntiReplayWindow instance use karta hai, toh ordering guarantee per-session hi rehti hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Ek lint rule ya wrapper add karna jo kisi aur jagah se record() ko directly call hone se roke (sirf Session.decrypt ke through allow kare). Mutation testing ko CI mein automate karna taaki yeh exact class of bug future changes mein bhi pakda jaaye.

question: Why does this project use InMemoryTunDevice plus real UDP sockets instead of requiring a real OS TUN device for every test?
answer_hinglish:
Real OS TUN device (`/dev/net/tun` Linux par) root/admin privileges maangta hai -- yeh environment aur owner ka Windows dev machine dono yeh nahi de sakte. Agar har test ko real TUN device chahiye hota, toh yeh project kahin test hi nahi ho sakta is setup mein.

InMemoryTunDevice ek honest substitute hai: poora encrypt/send/receive/decrypt path REAL hai -- real UDP loopback sockets, real ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD. Sirf EK part simulate hota hai: 'kernel ne packet route kiya aur TUN device tak pahunchaya' -- us part ko `send()`/`deliver()` directly call karke replace kiya jaata hai.

Yeh design decision README mein explicitly justify kiya gaya hai aur isi pattern ko repo ka ek doosra project (16-container-runtime) bhi follow karta hai, jahan jo root chahta tha woh sirf owner ke real Linux server par measure hua, environment mein nahi build hua. Trade-off clear hai: hum kernel-routing ko test nahi kar sakte, par crypto/protocol correctness (jo actual point hai) poori tarah real hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate test-environment constraints ko honestly handle kar sakta hai, bina feature ko fake claim kiye.
real_world_analogy: Flight simulator mein pilot training real controls, real physics ke saath hoti hai, bas plane khud zameen se udta nahi -- jo important skill hai (flying decisions) woh real hai, jo infrastructure chahiye (ek real runway/airport) woh simulate hota hai.
how_it_works: InMemoryTunDevice implements TunDevice's app-facing send()/onReceive(), plus an extra engine-facing onSend()/deliver() pair that VpnNode hooks into to drive the interface from both ends over real dgram sockets.
in_this_project: src/tun.ts ka InMemoryTunDevice; src/transport.ts ka VpnNode real node:dgram socket se wire hota hai. test/transport.test.ts aur test/invariants.test.ts dono isi combination par real UDP se chalte hain.
advantages: Entire crypto/protocol path is tested for real, over real sockets, no mocking of the hard parts
No root/admin privileges needed to run the full test suite anywhere
Same honest-substitution pattern already used elsewhere in this repo
disadvantages: Never exercises actual kernel TUN routing behavior or its edge cases
A bug specific to real TUN device I/O would not be caught by this test suite
Requires a clear mental model of which part is real (crypto/UDP) vs simulated (kernel routing)
common_mistakes: Assuming InMemoryTunDevice means the whole test suite is 'fake' -- only the kernel-routing step is simulated
Trying to add a real TUN device dependency without checking for root/admin availability first
Confusing TunDevice (app-facing interface) with InMemoryTunDevice's extra engine-facing methods
follow_up_questions: What specifically would change if a real Linux /dev/net/tun adapter were added later?
Why is onSend/deliver kept off the TunDevice interface itself and only on InMemoryTunDevice?
What's the honest limit of what this test setup can prove about a production deployment?

question: Why does this project derive a different key for each direction (i2r/r2i) instead of using one shared key for both send and receive?
answer_hinglish:
Agar EK shared key dono directions ke liye use hoti, toh dono peers ke counters EK hi nonce space share karte -- jaise hi Alice ne apna pehla packet bheja (counter 0) aur Bob ne apna pehla packet bheja (counter 0 bhi), dono SAME key ke saath SAME nonce (0) use kar lete. ChaCha20-Poly1305 jaise AEAD cipher ke liye yeh catastrophic hai -- same key+nonce pair do baar use karna poora confidentiality guarantee tod deta hai.

Isliye alag HKDF `info` labels use kiye gaye: `I2R_INFO` (initiator->responder) aur `R2I_INFO` (responder->initiator). Yeh dono labels SAME chained DH output (`dhSE`+`dhES`+`dhEE`) se but ALAG keys derive karte hain -- har direction ka apna independent counter hai, toh 'never reuse a nonce for a given key' rule trivially satisfy hoti hai.

Code mein dekho: `buildHandshakeResponse` responder ke liye `sendKey: hkdf(chain, R2I_INFO)` aur `recvKey: hkdf(chain, I2R_INFO)` return karta hai -- initiator ke liye yeh EXACTLY opposite assign hote hain (`openHandshakeResponse` mein `sendKey: hkdf(chain, I2R_INFO)`, `recvKey: hkdf(chain, R2I_INFO)`). Dono sides mirror hote hain -- jo ek side 'send' key hai woh doosri side ki 'recv' key hai, kabhi same direction ki key dono taraf 'send' nahi hoti.
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate AEAD nonce-reuse ke danger ko samajhta hai, aur isko key-separation se solve karne ka concrete pattern dekh sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Do log ek hi combination lock use karte hain apne apne alag lockers ke liye -- agar lock SAME combination se khulta hai aur dono apna counter zero se shuru karte, dono locker effectively same bhi khul jaate. Alag combination (alag key) rakhne se yeh clash hi nahi hota.
how_it_works: HKDF is called with two distinct `info` strings (I2R_INFO, R2I_INFO) over the same DH-chain input, producing two cryptographically independent keys -- one per direction, mirrored on each side.
in_this_project: src/handshake.ts ke I2R_INFO/R2I_INFO constants; buildHandshakeResponse aur openHandshakeResponse mirror karte hain kaunsi key 'send' hai kaunsi 'recv' -- Session constructor mein sendKey/recvKey alag Buffers hote hain.
advantages: Each direction has an independent counter/nonce space, making nonce reuse structurally impossible
A compromise of one direction's traffic analysis does not reveal anything extra about the other direction's key
Simple HKDF info-label separation, no extra cryptographic machinery needed
disadvantages: Two keys to manage instead of one, slightly more state per Session
Both sides must agree perfectly on which label means which direction, or the handshake silently fails to decrypt
Adds one more thing a mutation test needed to specifically cover (swapped labels would break decryption loudly, at least)
common_mistakes: Using a single shared key for both directions, enabling nonce reuse the moment both sides send one packet each
Swapping i2r/r2i labels on one side only, which breaks decryption (loudly, not silently)
Assuming HKDF's info label is just documentation rather than a real input that changes the derived key
follow_up_questions: What exact attack becomes possible if nonce 0 is reused under the same key in two different directions?
Why does swapping i2r/r2i on one side fail loudly rather than silently?
Would adding a third logical channel (e.g. control messages) need a third HKDF label -- why?

question: What would you need to add before this project could actually run as a real, deployed VPN rather than a learning exercise?
answer_hinglish:
README ke 'Known and NOT handled' section mein saari remaining gaps honestly listed hain, aur main unko priority order mein lagaunga. Sabse pehla: real OS TUN/TAP device -- abhi InMemoryTunDevice hai, jo root/admin maangta kernel device ke liye jo yeh environment nahi deta. Bina real TUN device ke, yeh koi actual network traffic carry nahi kar sakta.

Doosra: handshake-replay protection aur DoS-resistance cookie. Abhi ek captured HANDSHAKE_INIT replay ho sakta hai (harmless extra attempt, par repeated flood se CPU burn ho sakta hai) -- aur stage 2 ke baad har rekey ka HANDSHAKE_INIT bhi utna hi replayable hai. Production mein ek timestamp aur cookie/MAC mechanism chahiye, exactly jaisa real WireGuard karta hai.

Teesra: NAT traversal/endpoint roaming -- VpnNode peer ka address sirf handshake packets se seekhta hai aur fixed rakhta hai, real roaming support nahi hai.

Chautha: 64-bit counters abhi JS `number` se model hote hain (exact sirf 2^53 tak) -- genuinely high-throughput session ke liye `bigint` chahiye hoga (stage 2 ka `rekeyAfterMessages` isko practically avoid karne ka ek opt-in tarika deta hai, fix nahi).

Periodic rekeying is list mein ab nahi hai -- stage 2 mein built hai (current + retiring session, grace window, initiator-only, lost-handshake retry). Par deploy se pehle usko bhi tune karna padega: rekeyAfterMs ko minutes ke scale par set karna, VpnNode.startRekeyTimer chalana, aur lost-HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE path ka ek test add karna jo abhi nahi hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate production-readiness gaps ko systematically prioritize kar sakta hai, honest tareeke se, bina kisi ko miss kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek working prototype car engine ko real road par chalane se pehle brakes, headlights, aur registration chahiye -- engine already kaam karta hai, par 'drivable on a real road' banane ke liye aur bhi cheezein chahiye.
how_it_works: Each remaining gap maps to a specific missing mechanism: a real TUN adapter for kernel routing, a timestamp+cookie for handshake DoS resistance, address re-learning for roaming, and bigint counters for extreme-scale sessions. Rekeying is already implemented (Peer.checkRekey + VpnNode.startRekeyTimer) and only needs production tuning.
in_this_project: README.md ka 'Known and NOT handled' section aur PLAN.md ka 'Not in scope' paragraph (jo 'Still not in scope after stage 2' bhi list karta hai: handshake-replay protection, multi-peer concentrator, real /dev/net/tun adapter) isi list ko explicitly enumerate karte hain. Rekeying ke liye PLAN.md ka 'Stage 2 decisions' section.
advantages: Each gap is already individually documented, making the production roadmap concrete rather than vague
The core crypto/protocol layer (handshake, AEAD, anti-replay) needs no change -- gaps are additive
Dependency-injected pieces (VpnNode's tun parameter) make some additions (a real TUN adapter) a localized swap
disadvantages: Some gaps (roaming, a multi-peer concentrator) touch Peer/VpnNode state and are not purely additive
A real TUN adapter needs root/admin, so it cannot be validated in this environment at all
DoS-resistance cookie design itself is nontrivial and needs careful wire format changes
common_mistakes: Treating all gaps as equal priority instead of ranking by real deployment risk
Assuming a real TUN device is a small addition -- it changes the entire I/O model, not just one function
Listing rekeying as missing -- it is built in stage 2; what remains is tuning it (interval, timer, untested lost-response path), not designing it
follow_up_questions: Which of these four remaining gaps would you tackle first if you had one week, and why?
What would you tune about the existing stage-2 rekeying before real deployment?
What's the minimum DoS-resistance mechanism you'd add before exposing this to the public internet?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Prioritizing a real TUN adapter first makes the project actually USABLE, but a DoS cookie matters more for SAFETY under hostile traffic -- a real deployment facing the open internet should probably do DoS-hardening before or alongside the TUN adapter, since an unprotected handshake path is exploitable the moment the UDP port is reachable.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without a DoS cookie, an attacker floods HANDSHAKE_INIT messages; each one costs the responder an ECDH computation and a static-key decrypt attempt before being rejected -- at scale this is a real CPU exhaustion vector, not just 'harmless extra attempts'.
advanced.alternatives: Instead of building a cookie mechanism from scratch, a production deployment could sit this protocol behind an existing DoS-resistant proxy, trading implementation effort for an extra network hop and loss of end-to-end simplicity.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x peers, the in-memory sessionsByReceiverId map and bitmap windows scale fine (bounded per-session memory). At 100x+ concurrent peers, the single-threaded Node process and VpnNode's one-active-remote-peer scoping become the real bottleneck, not the crypto itself -- see the concentrator question for how that changes.
advanced.production_improvements: Add a real TUN adapter (Linux-only, root-gated), handshake cookie + timestamp (covering rekey handshakes too), address re-learning for roaming, and bigint counters for sessions expected to exceed 2^53 packets; for the already-built rekeying, set rekeyAfterMs to minutes, run VpnNode.startRekeyTimer, add jitter, and add a test for a lost rekey HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE.

question: If you were running this as a service, what would you monitor to catch a handshake failure rate problem before users complain?
answer_hinglish:
Main har `receiveHandshakeInit` aur `receiveHandshakeResponse` call ke reject-reason ko ek metric mein count karunga, broken down by reason: `AUTH_FAILED`, `UNTRUSTED_PEER`, `MALFORMED`, `NO_PENDING_HANDSHAKE`. Yeh dono methods already typed `{ok:false, reason}` return karte hain -- koi throw nahi hota -- toh instrumentation ek simple wrapper hai jo result ko inspect kare.

Ek SUDDEN spike in `AUTH_FAILED` ka matlab ho sakta hai ki kisi peer ki trusted static key config mismatch ho gayi hai (jaise ek rotated key doosri side update nahi hui), ya kisi ne wrong key configure kar diya. `UNTRUSTED_PEER` spike ka matlab shayad ek naya peer try kar raha hai jiski key abhi `trustPeer()` se register nahi hui -- ya ek genuine attack attempt.

Ek baseline rate (normal operation mein kitna % handshake fail hota hai, usually network blips ya race conditions se) establish karna zaroori hai, taaki alert sirf DEVIATION par fire ho, absolute number par nahi. VpnNode ka `onDropped` callback already har rejection ko ek string reason ke saath emit karta hai -- production mein yeh ek structured metric (counter + label) mein convert hoga instead of console.log.
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate typed rejection values ko observability signal mein convert karna jaanta hai, aur baseline-vs-deviation monitoring philosophy samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek building ke entry gate par security log rakhta hai kitne log 'wrong ID' ya 'unrecognized visitor' ke wajah se reject hue -- sudden spike dikhata hai ki kuch unusual ho raha hai, chahe woh ek system glitch ho ya koi intrusion attempt.
how_it_works: Wrap receiveHandshakeInit/receiveHandshakeResponse results: on {ok:false, reason}, increment a counter metric labeled by reason; alert on rate-of-change against a rolling baseline, not a fixed absolute threshold.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts ka HandshakeInitResult/HandshakeResponseResult types; src/transport.ts ka onDropped callback already string reasons emit karta hai jo isi metric ka starting point ban sakta hai.
advantages: Typed rejection reasons already give clean, stable metric labels without string parsing
No throw-based control flow to work around -- observability wraps cleanly around the existing API
Different reasons point to different root causes, so one metric with a label dimension covers all of them
disadvantages: A single aggregate 'handshake failure rate' metric without the reason breakdown would hide the actual cause
Baseline-based alerting needs enough historical data to be meaningful, which a brand-new deployment lacks
Does not by itself distinguish a misconfiguration from a deliberate attack -- needs correlation with source addresses
common_mistakes: Alerting on absolute failure count instead of rate-of-change against a baseline
Logging failures as unstructured text instead of a labeled metric, making dashboards hard to build
Treating AUTH_FAILED and UNTRUSTED_PEER as the same signal when they point to different root causes
follow_up_questions: How would you distinguish a key-rotation misconfiguration from an actual attack using only this metric?
What additional dimension (besides reason) would you want on this metric in a multi-peer deployment?
Would you alert per-peer or in aggregate, and why?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Putting the metric at the Peer level (inside receiveHandshakeInit/Response) versus at the VpnNode's onDropped level is a real choice: Peer-level is closer to the actual decision and works even without a transport layer, but onDropped already has a string reason and is the simpler integration point for a first version.
advanced.failure_scenarios: A rotated static key on one side without updating trustPeer() on the other produces a sustained, not transient, spike in AUTH_FAILED or UNTRUSTED_PEER -- the signal should distinguish a brief blip (network issue) from a sustained plateau (configuration drift).
advanced.alternatives: Instead of counters, a sampled trace/log of failed handshakes (with peer name, reason, timestamp) gives richer debugging context at a higher storage cost -- a production system would likely want both: counters for alerting, sampled logs for investigation.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x peers, per-peer breakdown is still manageable. At 100x+ peers, a single aggregate failure-rate metric becomes too coarse to localize the problem -- you need per-peer or per-peer-group cardinality, which raises metric storage cost and requires careful label cardinality limits.
advanced.production_improvements: Emit structured metrics with reason as a label, add a sampled failure log for investigation, and build an alert that compares current failure rate against a rolling 24h baseline rather than a fixed threshold.

question: Why would a rising replay-drop rate matter for monitoring, and what could actually be causing it in production?
answer_hinglish:
`AntiReplayWindow.check()` jab REPLAY return karta hai, Session.decrypt() usko `{ok:false, reason:'REPLAY'}` bana deta hai -- yeh VpnNode ke `onDropped` callback tak pahunchta hai 'transport packet dropped: REPLAY' string ke saath. Isko ek metric mein count karna zaroori hai kyunki REPLAY rate ka matlab ho sakta hai do bahut alag cheezein.

Pehla, benign cause: network-level packet duplication -- kuch UDP paths (especially agar koi middlebox retransmit kar raha ho) genuinely duplicate packets deliver kar sakte hain, aur anti-replay sahi se unhe drop kar raha hai -- yeh EXPECTED behavior hai, koi bug nahi.

Doosra, concerning cause: ek ACTUAL replay attack -- koi captured packets ko intentionally resend kar raha hai. Dono cases mein metric same dikhega (REPLAY count badh raha hai), isliye context chahiye: kya yeh EK specific peer se aa raha hai sudden burst mein (suspicious), ya spread across many peers consistently (likely network characteristic)?

Ek aur subtle case: agar window size (2048) bahut chhota hai production ke actual packet reordering/jitter ke against, toh legitimate OUT-OF-ORDER packets bhi kabhi-kabhi TOO_OLD reject ho sakte hain (REPLAY nahi, but related) -- yeh distinguish karna zaroori hai REPLAY vs TOO_OLD counts alag track karke.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek single metric ke multiple possible root causes ko distinguish kar sakta hai, aur benign-vs-attack scenarios ko reason kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek toll booth par duplicate ticket scan hona ya to ek genuine double-scan glitch ho sakta hai, ya koi ticket photocopy karke dobara use karne ki koshish kar raha ho -- same symptom, do bahut alag explanations.
how_it_works: Session.decrypt() returns {ok:false, reason:'REPLAY'} when AntiReplayWindow.check() finds the counter already seen; this surfaces through VpnNode.onDropped as a droppable string, which should become a labeled counter metric distinguishing REPLAY from TOO_OLD.
in_this_project: src/replay-window.ts ka ReplayCheck type ('ACCEPT'|'REPLAY'|'TOO_OLD'); src/session.ts ka decrypt() method jo check() ke result ko directly reason bana deta hai.
advantages: REPLAY and TOO_OLD are already distinct typed values, so metric labeling needs no extra logic
Per-peer breakdown (via peerName already available in Peer's decryptPacket) localizes the problem quickly
A rising rate is cheap to detect since it is already a counted, discrete event
disadvantages: Cannot by itself distinguish benign network duplication from a deliberate replay attack
A too-small window size would also produce TOO_OLD noise that looks superficially similar
Needs correlation with network path / peer identity to be actionable, not just a raw count
common_mistakes: Treating any nonzero replay rate as an attack without considering normal network duplication
Not separating REPLAY from TOO_OLD, which have different root causes (attack/duplication vs window sizing)
Alerting without a per-peer breakdown, missing that the problem is isolated to one peer
follow_up_questions: How would you tell apart a replay attack from benign network-level packet duplication using this metric?
What would a rising TOO_OLD rate (not REPLAY) suggest about window sizing in production?
Would you alert on absolute rate or rate relative to total transport packets?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Separating REPLAY and TOO_OLD into distinct metrics costs one extra label dimension but makes the signal far more actionable -- collapsing them into one 'drop' metric would make window-sizing problems look identical to attacks, which is strictly worse for on-call diagnosis.
advanced.failure_scenarios: A real replay attack typically shows as a burst from one source re-sending a small set of exact ciphertexts; benign duplication from flaky network paths tends to be spread more evenly and proportional to total traffic -- the SHAPE of the metric over time (not just its value) is the real diagnostic signal.
advanced.alternatives: Instead of only a rate metric, logging the actual counter value on each REPLAY (sampled, not every one) lets you see whether the same counter keeps repeating (attack signature) versus many different nearby counters (jitter/duplication).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x traffic, a global replay-rate metric is fine. At 100x+ traffic across many peers, you need per-peer cardinality to avoid one noisy peer masking a real attack against another -- and the underlying AntiReplayWindow's O(size) per-session memory cost becomes a real aggregate memory line item worth tracking.
advanced.production_improvements: Separate REPLAY/TOO_OLD metrics with peer-name labels, sampled logging of repeated counters for attack-pattern detection, and a review of window size against measured real-world reordering/jitter before tuning alerts.

question: What would a sudden rise in AEAD-auth-failure rate tell an on-call engineer, and how would they investigate it?
answer_hinglish:
AEAD-auth-failure (`AUTH_FAILED` reason) tab aata hai jab `aeadDecrypt()` throw karta hai -- ciphertext, tag, ya AAD mein se kuch bhi mismatch hota hai expected value se. Session.decrypt() isko catch karke typed rejection bana deta hai, kabhi crash nahi hota.

Investigation ka pehla step: kya yeh EK specific peer/session se aa raha hai, ya WIDESPREAD hai. Agar widespread hai, sabse likely cause ek BUG hai (jaise koi recent deploy jisne key derivation ya AAD construction galat kar diya) -- is case mein main recent deploys/changes check karunga pehle.

Agar EK specific peer/session se isolated hai, toh possibilities: (1) network corruption genuinely tamper kar raha hai bytes ko beech mein (rare but possible on lossy links), (2) koi actual tampering attack ho raha hai, ya (3) dono sides ki Session state kisi tareeke se desync ho gayi (jaise ek side ne galat key install kar li -- yeh is project mein theoretically nahi hona chahiye given handshake correctness, par worth checking).

Log mein `transportAad(receiverId, counter)` values compare karna helpful hai -- agar AAD field KHUD corrupt hua (jaise receiverId ya counter truncated), decrypt bhi fail karega bina ciphertext tamper hue. Isliye AUTH_FAILED sirf ciphertext tamper ka proof nahi, AAD mismatch ka bhi ho sakta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate ek symptom (auth failure) ko systematic debugging steps mein tod sakta hai -- bug vs attack vs network corruption.
real_world_analogy: Ek bank cheque ka signature match nahi ho raha -- yeh forgery ho sakti hai, ya printer ne cheque ka format thoda galat print kar diya ho (same symptom, alag causes), investigation dono possibilities check karta hai.
how_it_works: aeadDecrypt() throws on any mismatch (ciphertext, tag, or AAD); Session.decrypt() catches this and returns {ok:false, reason:'AUTH_FAILED'} rather than crashing or silently succeeding with wrong data.
in_this_project: src/crypto-utils.ts ka aeadDecrypt() function (throws on tag mismatch); src/session.ts ka decrypt() method ka try/catch block jo AUTH_FAILED return karta hai.
advantages: AUTH_FAILED is a single, unambiguous typed reason -- never a silent wrong-data success
Isolating by peer/session quickly separates 'widespread bug' from 'isolated issue'
AAD construction is deterministic, making field-corruption vs ciphertext-tamper distinguishable by careful logging
disadvantages: AUTH_FAILED alone cannot distinguish a deploy bug from a genuine tampering attempt without more context
No built-in logging of which AAD field might be the mismatch source -- that investigation is manual today
A widespread-vs-isolated distinction requires good per-peer breakdown, which must be built, not assumed
common_mistakes: Assuming every AUTH_FAILED is an attack rather than first checking for a recent bad deploy
Not checking whether the failure is isolated to one peer versus affecting all sessions equally
Forgetting that AAD field corruption (not just ciphertext tamper) can also trigger AUTH_FAILED
follow_up_questions: What's the first thing you'd check if AUTH_FAILED suddenly spiked across ALL sessions at once?
How would you distinguish an AAD corruption bug from an actual tampered-ciphertext attack from logs alone?
Would you page someone immediately on this metric, or wait for a sustained trend -- why?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Catching the AEAD exception inside Session.decrypt() (rather than letting it propagate) trades some debugging detail (the exact byte that mismatched is lost) for a clean, never-crashes receive-side contract -- a production system would want a DEBUG-level log with more detail behind this catch, not in the hot path return value itself.
advanced.failure_scenarios: A widespread AUTH_FAILED spike right after a deploy almost always means a key-derivation or AAD-construction regression; an isolated spike on one peer over a flaky link is more likely genuine network corruption, since AEAD's tag is designed to catch even single-bit flips reliably.
advanced.alternatives: Instead of only a boolean-style typed rejection, a production variant could log (at low sample rate) a hash of the mismatched AAD/ciphertext for forensic comparison -- balancing debuggability against the risk of logging sensitive-adjacent data.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x traffic, per-session auth-failure tracking is easy. At 100x+ sessions, you need aggregation that still lets you drill into 'which specific peer' without storing per-packet detail for every single packet -- sampling becomes necessary.
advanced.production_improvements: Add a debug-level log (sampled) capturing enough context (peer name, counter, which AAD fields) to distinguish bug-vs-attack without logging raw ciphertext at scale; dashboard AUTH_FAILED rate split by peer and correlate with deploy timestamps automatically.

question: An on-call engineer gets paged with 'VPN keeps dropping packets.' Walk through how you'd investigate this using only what this project exposes.
answer_hinglish:
Sabse pehla step: `VpnNode.onDropped` callback ke reasons dekho -- yeh already ek human-readable string deta hai jaise 'transport packet dropped: REPLAY' ya 'handshake init rejected: AUTH_FAILED'. Yeh ek single entry point hai jo HAR drop reason ko surface karta hai, toh main pehle yeh dekhunga ki dominant reason kya hai.

Agar dominant reason REPLAY hai: check karo kya yeh ek specific peer se concentrated hai (possible attack ya duplicate-sending bug upstream) ya spread across sab (network-level duplication, shayad window size tuning ki zaroorat hai).

Agar dominant reason AUTH_FAILED hai TRANSPORT packets par (not handshake): check karo kya yeh recent deploy ke baad shuru hua -- agar haan, key-derivation ya AAD-construction regression likely hai. Agar isolated hai, network corruption ya tampering check karo.

Agar dominant reason UNKNOWN_SESSION hai: iska matlab packets ek receiverId ke saath aa rahe hain jiske liye koi Session installed nahi hai -- yeh suggest karta hai ki HANDSHAKE kabhi complete nahi hua ya Session establish hone se pehle hi packets bheje gaye (race condition), ya VpnNode restart hua aur purani sessions memory se gayab ho gayi (kyunki sab in-memory hai).

Agar dominant reason handshake-side hai (UNTRUSTED_PEER/MALFORMED), toh yeh 'drop' nahi, yeh 'connection never established' hai -- root cause configuration mein hai, data path mein nahi. Har case mein `onDropped` ka string reason hi primary diagnostic signal hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek vague symptom ko systematic investigation mein tod sakta hai using sirf jo tools/signals project actually expose karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek customer complain karta hai 'internet slow hai' -- support engineer pehle specific error codes/logs dekhta hai (timeout? DNS fail? packet loss?) instead of randomly guess karne ke, exactly jaisa yahan onDropped reason categorize karta hai.
how_it_works: VpnNode.onDropped(callback) fires with a human-readable reason string on every rejected handshake message or transport packet; triaging starts by bucketing these reasons and checking per-peer concentration versus system-wide spread.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts ka onDropped/emitDropped mechanism aur handleMessage method -- yahi single place hai jahan har rejection path converge karta hai aur reason string banta hai.
advantages: A single onDropped callback already centralizes every rejection reason, no scattered logging to correlate
Reasons are specific enough (REPLAY, AUTH_FAILED, UNKNOWN_SESSION, etc.) to immediately narrow the investigation
Distinguishing handshake-side drops from transport-side drops separates 'never connected' from 'connected but losing packets'
disadvantages: onDropped gives no peer-address or timestamp context by itself -- the callback body must add that
Strings, not structured labels, mean a production system would still need to parse/categorize them
No built-in historical aggregation -- this is a live callback, not a queryable metric store
common_mistakes: Investigating without first categorizing which specific reason dominates the drops
Treating a handshake rejection the same as a transport packet drop -- they mean very different things
Assuming UNKNOWN_SESSION means an attack when a restart (losing in-memory state) is a much more common cause
follow_up_questions: What would you add to onDropped's signature to make this triage faster in production?
Why would UNKNOWN_SESSION specifically point you toward a process restart or race condition?
How would you distinguish 'packets are being dropped' from 'the handshake never completed in the first place'?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Centralizing all rejections through one onDropped callback (rather than separate callbacks per failure type) trades some type-safety for a single, easy-to-wire observability seam -- a production system would likely want this plus structured fields (peer, reason, timestamp) rather than a bare string, but the single-seam design is still the right starting shape.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If VpnNode restarts (process crash/redeploy), every session is gone (in-memory only) -- any peer that doesn't re-handshake will see 100% UNKNOWN_SESSION drops until a new handshake completes; this looks alarming but has an ordinary operational cause.
advanced.alternatives: Instead of triaging from a live callback, a production system would want these reasons flowing into a time-series metrics store so an on-call engineer can see the SHAPE of the problem (sudden step change vs gradual trend) before even looking at live logs.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x peers, manually watching onDropped output is still feasible for debugging. At 100x+ peers, this needs to become metrics with per-peer cardinality and a dashboard, since no human can watch a raw callback stream at that volume.
advanced.production_improvements: Convert onDropped's string reasons into structured, labeled metrics; add peer address and timestamp to every drop event; build a runbook mapping each reason to its likely root causes, exactly as walked through here.

question: How would you think about capacity planning if a single server needed to hold many concurrent peer sessions using this design?
answer_hinglish:
Capacity planning ke liye sabse pehla cost per-session memory hai. Har `Session` apna `AntiReplayWindow` rakhta hai -- default `size=2048` bits, matlab `2048/8 = 256` bytes ka bitmap per session, plus do 32-byte keys (sendKey, recvKey) aur ek counter. Roughly ~350-400 bytes per session SIRF yeh state ke liye, excluding JS object overhead.

`Peer` class teen maps maintain karta hai: `peerSessions`, `sessionsByReceiverId`, `trustedByName`/`trustedByKeyHex`. Yeh sab O(1) lookups hain, toh CPU cost per-packet nahi badhta jaise peer count badhta hai -- memory hi primary scaling constraint hai, lookup speed nahi.

`VpnNode` abhi POINT-TO-POINT scoped hai (ek active remote peer per node) -- yeh current design 'many concurrent peer sessions on one server' handle NAHI karta as-is; `Peer` class khud multiple peers support karta hai (trust + sessions), par `VpnNode`'s `activePeerName` aur `tun.send()` ka ambiguity-free destination assumption single-peer ko assume karta hai. Is design ko concentrator banane ke liye (VPN-122 dekho), per-packet dispatch logic add karni padegi.

Real capacity number estimate karne ke liye: `(memory budget) / (~400 bytes + object overhead)` per session, plus UDP socket buffer limits aur single-threaded Node event loop ka per-packet processing cost (encrypt/decrypt CPU time) jo actual throughput ceiling set karta hai, memory se pehle.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate per-resource cost breakdown kar sakta hai (memory vs CPU vs architectural limit) aur honestly identify kar sakta hai ki current design kya already support karta hai vs kya extend karna padega.
real_world_analogy: Ek hotel capacity planning karte waqt sirf rooms count nahi karti -- staff, kitchen throughput, aur parking bhi alag constraints hain; jo pehle bottleneck ho woh REAL capacity limit set karta hai, chahe rooms kaafi hon.
how_it_works: Per-session memory = AntiReplayWindow bitmap (size/8 bytes) + two 32-byte keys + counter state; Peer's maps give O(1) lookup regardless of peer count; VpnNode's point-to-point scoping is the actual architectural ceiling for a single-server multi-peer deployment, not memory.
in_this_project: src/replay-window.ts ke constructor ka bitmap allocation; src/peer.ts ke peerSessions/sessionsByReceiverId maps; src/transport.ts ka activePeerName (point-to-point scoping).
advantages: Session memory cost is small and fixed per session, making memory-based capacity math straightforward
Peer's map-based lookups mean CPU cost per packet does not grow with total session count
The architectural ceiling (point-to-point VpnNode) is clearly identified rather than hidden
disadvantages: VpnNode's current design cannot actually host many concurrent peers without being extended into a concentrator
Single-threaded Node event loop means CPU-bound AEAD work, not memory, is likely the real throughput ceiling at scale
No built-in session eviction/cleanup -- idle sessions stay in memory indefinitely, inflating the memory estimate over time
common_mistakes: Assuming Peer's multi-peer support means VpnNode already supports many concurrent peers (it does not, by design)
Only counting bitmap memory and forgetting the two session keys and JS object/Map overhead
Ignoring CPU cost of AEAD encrypt/decrypt as a scaling factor and focusing only on memory
follow_up_questions: What architectural change would let a single server actually host many concurrent peers?
At what session count would AEAD CPU cost likely overtake memory as the bottleneck?
Would you add session eviction for idle peers, and how would you decide the idle threshold?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Keeping VpnNode point-to-point simplified the demo and tests at the cost of not being directly capacity-plannable for 'many peers on one server' -- that capability lives conceptually in Peer already, so extending VpnNode into a concentrator is additive work, not a redesign of the protocol layer.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If a server's session count grows without any eviction policy, memory grows unboundedly even for peers that stopped sending traffic long ago -- eventually this becomes an OOM risk, not a gradual slowdown, since there's no backpressure signal in this design today.
advanced.alternatives: Horizontal scaling (many single-purpose VpnNode-like processes, each handling a subset of peers, behind a load balancer keyed by peer identity) avoids the concentrator rewrite entirely, at the cost of needing session-affinity routing.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x sessions, current per-session memory cost is a rounding error. At 100x-1000x, bitmap + key memory becomes a real line item (hundreds of MB), and single-threaded AEAD CPU cost becomes the dominant constraint well before memory does -- multi-process or worker-thread sharding would be needed.
advanced.production_improvements: Add idle-session eviction with a configurable timeout, convert VpnNode into (or wrap it with) a multi-peer concentrator, and benchmark actual AEAD throughput per core to set a realistic sessions-per-server number instead of estimating from memory alone.

question: This project explicitly has no DoS-resistance cookie for the handshake. What concrete attack does that gap enable, and what's the minimal fix?
answer_hinglish:
Gap README mein explicitly documented hai: 'a captured HANDSHAKE_INIT CAN be replayed, producing a harmless extra handshake attempt... nothing stops an attacker from doing this repeatedly to burn CPU.' Concrete attack: attacker ek valid-looking HANDSHAKE_INIT (apna khud ya captured) bar-bar bhejta hai responder ko. Har attempt par responder `openHandshakeInit` call karta hai -- yeh EK ECDH computation (`ecdh(responderStaticPrivate, ...)`) aur EK AEAD decrypt attempt karta hai, dono non-trivial CPU cost. High-volume flood se yeh CPU exhaust kar sakta hai, legitimate handshakes ko delay/starve kar sakta hai.

Minimal fix (jo WireGuard khud use karta hai): ek stateless 'cookie' mechanism jahan responder, suspected-under-load state mein, pehle ek lightweight cookie-reply bhejta hai jo initiator ko wapas proof-of-work jaisa kuch karna padta hai (ya simply ek MAC jo initiator ko apna HELLO ke saath echo karna padta hai) -- yeh ek EXPENSIVE ECDH computation se pehle hi fake/non-returning attackers ko filter kar deta hai, kyunki woh cookie ka exchange ek genuine UDP round-trip require karta hai jo IP-spoofed attacker nahi complete kar sakta.

Is project mein abhi `openHandshakeInit` directly costly computation kar deta hai bina kisi pre-filter ke -- production fix is function se PEHLE ek cheap, stateless check insert karega.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek documented limitation ko concrete attack scenario mein translate kar sakta hai aur ek realistic, minimal mitigation propose kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek office reception bina appointment verify kiye directly har visitor ko CEO ke office tak le jaata hai -- yeh fast lagta hai par ek flood of fake visitors CEO ka pura din burn kar sakte hain; ek simple sign-in sheet check pehle hi fake visitors ko filter kar deta.
how_it_works: openHandshakeInit performs an ECDH computation and an AEAD decrypt attempt for EVERY received message, with no pre-filter; a cookie mechanism would require a cheap round-trip proof before that expensive work runs, filtering out attackers that cannot complete a real UDP handshake.
in_this_project: src/handshake.ts ka openHandshakeInit function -- yeh har call par unconditionally ecdh() aur aeadDecrypt() karta hai, koi rate-limit ya cookie check nahi.
advantages: The attack surface is precisely identified -- unconditional ECDH + AEAD decrypt cost per received init message
A cookie mechanism is a well-understood, proven pattern (real WireGuard uses exactly this)
The fix can be inserted as a pre-check before openHandshakeInit, without redesigning the core handshake
disadvantages: Adding a cookie mechanism changes the wire format and adds a round trip under load, affecting latency
Determining WHEN to switch into cookie-required mode (load-based threshold) is itself a design decision
IP-spoofing resistance of the cookie depends on getting the stateless MAC design right
common_mistakes: Assuming rate-limiting by source IP alone is sufficient (spoofed/rotating source IPs defeat this)
Adding the cookie check only sometimes instead of consistently gating the expensive path
Underestimating that ECDH, not just AEAD, is the expensive operation being exploited
follow_up_questions: Why does a stateless cookie specifically resist IP-spoofed attackers better than a per-IP rate limiter?
What would the wire format need to carry to support a cookie-reply message?
At what load threshold would you switch a responder into 'cookie required' mode?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Adding a cookie mechanism unconditionally (always required) simplifies the design but adds a round trip to every single handshake even under normal load; WireGuard's actual approach only requires the cookie when the responder detects it is under load, trading implementation complexity for better normal-case latency.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without this fix, a sustained flood of HANDSHAKE_INIT messages (even from a single source, since no rate limit exists either) can starve the CPU budget available for legitimate initiators' ECDH computations, causing real handshakes to time out even though nothing has 'crashed'.
advanced.alternatives: A simpler, less complete mitigation would be a per-source-IP rate limiter in front of the UDP socket -- cheaper to build, but defeated by an attacker that spoofs or rotates source IPs, which a stateless cookie is specifically designed to resist.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At low attack volume, even the current unprotected design tolerates occasional replayed inits fine. At attack volumes approaching what a real botnet could generate, the unconditional ECDH-per-message cost becomes the single largest DoS risk in this entire system, well above anything in the transport/anti-replay path.
advanced.production_improvements: Implement a load-triggered stateless cookie exchange before the expensive ECDH+decrypt path runs, add a basic per-source-IP rate limiter as a cheap first layer, and monitor handshake-attempt rate as a leading indicator before CPU saturation actually occurs.

question: Trace the exact control flow of initiateHandshake on the initiator side through to a completed Session on BOTH sides.
answer_hinglish:
Alice (initiator) `initiateHandshake('bob')` call karti hai. Yeh pehle `trustedByName.get('bob')` se bob ki believed static key nikalta hai (throw `UNKNOWN_PEER` agar missing), phir `pendingHandshakes` mein already-pending check karta hai (throw `HANDSHAKE_IN_PROGRESS` agar mila). Fresh ephemeral keypair aur random `initiatorReceiverId` banta hai, `buildHandshakeInit()` call hoti hai jo `dhSE = ecdh(ephemeral.priv, bob's believed static pub)` compute karti hai aur message 1 encode karti hai. Yeh state `pendingHandshakes.set(initiatorReceiverId, {...})` mein save hoti hai, aur message bytes return hoti hain.

Bob (responder) `receiveHandshakeInit(msg1)` call karta hai. `openHandshakeInit()` same `dhSE` apni taraf se recompute karta hai (`ecdh(bob's static priv, Alice's ephemeral pub)` -- algebraically equal), decrypt karta hai Alice ki claimed static key. `trustedByKeyHex.get(...)` se peerName resolve hota hai (UNTRUSTED_PEER agar na mile). Fresh responder ephemeral banta hai, `buildHandshakeResponse()` teen DH terms chain karti hai (dhSE+dhES+dhEE), session keys derive karti hai, aur `installSession()` IMMEDIATELY Bob ki taraf session install kar deta hai -- Bob yahin se 'done' hai.

Alice `receiveHandshakeResponse(msg2)` call karti hai. `pendingHandshakes.get(initiatorReceiverId)` se pending state nikalta hai (NO_PENDING_HANDSHAKE agar missing), `openHandshakeResponse()` same chain recompute karta hai aur msg2's confirmation tag verify karta hai. Success par `pendingHandshakes.delete()` aur `installSession()` -- Alice ka session bhi ab ready hai. Dono sides ab `hasSession()` true return karte hain.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate end-to-end flow ko function-by-function trace kar sakta hai, including state transitions (pendingHandshakes -> installed session) dono sides par.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier ek registered letter bhejta hai (initiate), receiver sign karke acknowledgment bhejta hai (response) -- par yahan dono taraf letter ke andar ek 'proof' hai jo sirf tab valid hota hai jab dono ki keys sahi match karti hain.
how_it_works: initiateHandshake builds message 1 and stores pending state; receiveHandshakeInit decrypts it, verifies trust, and installs the RESPONDER's session immediately; receiveHandshakeResponse verifies message 2 against the stored pending state and installs the INITIATOR's session, clearing the pending entry.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts ke initiateHandshake, receiveHandshakeInit, receiveHandshakeResponse, aur private installSession methods -- yeh exact sequence test/peer.test.ts ke handshake() helper function mein directly reproduce hoti hai.
advantages: Responder completes its half of the session the moment it sends message 2, with no further waiting
Pending state is keyed by a random receiver id, so concurrent handshakes with different peers never collide
Every step either throws (send side) or returns a typed rejection (receive side), with no ambiguous states
disadvantages: The responder is 'done' before confirming the initiator actually received message 2 -- a lost message 2 leaves the responder with a session the initiator doesn't have yet
pendingHandshakes must be correctly cleared on success (mutation P5's exact bug) or future handshakes with the same peer get wrongly blocked
No timeout/cleanup for a pending handshake that never completes at the Peer level (VpnNode adds this at the transport layer)
common_mistakes: Assuming both sides complete the handshake at the same moment -- the responder finishes first
Forgetting that dhSE must be preserved from message 1 build time to message 2 processing time
Not clearing pendingHandshakes on success, permanently blocking a later re-handshake
follow_up_questions: What happens if message 2 (the response) is lost in transit after Bob has already installed his session?
Why does Bob install his session before knowing Alice received the response?
What would you add to detect a handshake that is stuck pending forever?

question: Walk through exactly how the HKDF info labels I2R_INFO and R2I_INFO are used in code to produce mirrored, non-colliding keys on both sides.
answer_hinglish:
`I2R_INFO = "mini-vpn transport i2r"` aur `R2I_INFO = "mini-vpn transport r2i"` -- yeh plain strings hain jo `hkdf(chain, info)` ke second argument ban jaate hain. `chain` (teen DH outputs ka concatenation) SAME dono sides par hota hai, par `info` string alag hone se `hkdfSync` completely ALAG output key deta hai (HKDF ka design yahi guarantee karta hai: alag info = alag independent key, chahe input material same ho).

Responder side (`buildHandshakeResponse`): `sendKey: hkdf(chain, R2I_INFO)` (responder->initiator traffic ke liye), `recvKey: hkdf(chain, I2R_INFO)` (initiator->responder traffic decrypt karne ke liye).

Initiator side (`openHandshakeResponse`): EXACT MIRROR -- `sendKey: hkdf(chain, I2R_INFO)` (initiator->responder), `recvKey: hkdf(chain, R2I_INFO)` (responder->initiator). Dekho: jo responder ki 'recvKey' hai (I2R) woh initiator ki 'sendKey' hai -- same key, dono sides mein opposite role mein use hoti hai.

Yeh labeling discipline hi ensure karti hai ki Alice jo encrypt karti hai apni sendKey se, Bob usko apni recvKey se decrypt kar sake -- aur dono NEVER same key apne 'send' ke liye use karein, jo nonce-space collision avoid karta hai (VPN-107 dekho).
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate HKDF ke 'info' parameter ko sirf documentation nahi, balki ek real cryptographic input samajhta hai jo output key ko completely change karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek hi master recipe (chain) se do bawarchi alag labeled dishes banate hain ('starter' label se ek dish, 'dessert' label se doosri) -- same base ingredients, par label change karne se poora alag output banta hai.
how_it_works: hkdf(ikm, info, length) feeds `info` as HKDF's context-separation input; buildHandshakeResponse and openHandshakeResponse assign I2R_INFO/R2I_INFO to opposite sendKey/recvKey roles so each side's send key equals the other side's recv key.
in_this_project: src/handshake.ts ke I2R_INFO/R2I_INFO constants aur buildHandshakeResponse/openHandshakeResponse mein unki mirrored assignment; src/crypto-utils.ts ka hkdf() function jo info ko hkdfSync ke info param mein directly pass karta hai.
advantages: HKDF's info-label separation needs no extra state -- the same chain input deterministically yields distinct keys
Mirrored assignment on both sides is simple enough to visually audit for correctness
A wrong label assignment fails loudly (decryption fails) rather than silently corrupting data
disadvantages: A typo swapping I2R_INFO and R2I_INFO on just one side would break decryption in a way that looks like a generic AUTH_FAILED, not an obviously labeled bug
Requires both MSG1_INFO/MSG2_INFO and I2R_INFO/R2I_INFO to all stay distinct -- four labels to keep straight
The labels themselves are just strings; nothing in the type system enforces they can't collide
common_mistakes: Assuming info is purely cosmetic/documentation rather than an actual cryptographic separator
Mirroring the labels incorrectly (both sides using I2R_INFO for sendKey) which would make both sides decrypt with the SAME key, defeating direction separation
Reusing MSG2_INFO (the handshake confirmation key label) for transport keys by mistake
follow_up_questions: What would actually happen (test-observably) if both sides used I2R_INFO for their own sendKey?
Why must MSG1_INFO/MSG2_INFO be distinct from I2R_INFO/R2I_INFO even though they're all derived from related DH material?
How does HKDF guarantee that two different info strings over the same ikm produce independent-looking keys?

question: Walk through exactly how AntiReplayWindow's bitmap bit-indexing works for an out-of-order counter -- which bit gets checked and why that's safe.
answer_hinglish:
`slot(counter) = counter % size` -- yeh counter ko ek fixed-size bitmap (default 2048 bits) ke andar ek bit-index mein map karta hai. `isSet(counter)`: `bit = slot(counter)`, phir `bitmap[bit >> 3] & (1 << (bit & 7))` -- `bit >> 3` byte-index nikalta hai (8 bits per byte), `bit & 7` us byte ke andar ka bit-position (0-7) nikalta hai.

Out-of-order counter ka example: suppose `highest = 100`, `size = 2048`, aur counter `95` abhi aata hai (late, par window ke andar hai kyunki `95 > highest - size`). `check(95)`: `95 <= highest` hai (100 se chhota), toh yeh seedha `isSet(95)` check karta hai -- `slot(95) = 95 % 2048 = 95`. Agar woh bit clear hai, ACCEPT; set hai, REPLAY.

Yeh SAFE hai kyunki `record()` ka slide-forward logic guarantee karta hai ki jab bhi window aage badhti hai, EVERY slot jo naye range mein enter karta hai pehle `clear()` ho jaata hai -- isliye modulo wraparound ka risk (ek purana, OUT-OF-WINDOW counter ka stale bit kisi naye counter ke SAME slot mein galti se 'already seen' dikhana) nahi hota, kyunki `check()` pehle hi `counter <= highest - size` wale cases ko TOO_OLD maar deta hai, bitmap tak pahunchne se pehle hi.
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate bit-level indexing (byte/bit split) aur usko surrounding safety invariant (TOO_OLD guard + clear-on-slide) se kaise connected hai, dono samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek circular parking lot mein spot number `car_id % total_spots` se decide hota hai -- agar woh spot already occupied hai SAME cycle mein, duplicate hai; par agar pehle wali car bahut purani thi (poora circle ho gaya), uska spot pehle hi clear ho chuka hoga naye occupant ke liye.
how_it_works: slot(counter) = counter % size maps a counter to a fixed bit position; isSet reads `bitmap[bit>>3] & (1<<(bit&7))`; the TOO_OLD check in check() runs BEFORE this, preventing stale-slot collisions from ever being misread as a real replay.
in_this_project: src/replay-window.ts ke slot(), isSet(), set(), clear() private methods aur check()'s TOO_OLD early-return, jo bitmap ko hamesha consistent rakhte hain.
advantages: Bit-packed storage keeps memory tiny (size/8 bytes) regardless of how many counters have been seen
Modulo-based slotting makes lookup O(1) with simple arithmetic, no hashing needed
TOO_OLD guard running before the bitmap read closes the one hole that modulo wraparound would otherwise open
disadvantages: The safety of this indexing depends entirely on record()'s clear-on-slide discipline being correct -- a bug there (mutation R4) breaks the whole scheme silently
Choosing the wrong window size relative to real reordering can cause legitimate packets to read as TOO_OLD
Bit-twiddling code (>>3, &7) is less self-documenting than a higher-level data structure would be
common_mistakes: Reading isSet() without first checking TOO_OLD, risking a stale-slot false positive/negative
Getting the byte/bit split backwards (e.g. >>3 vs &7 swapped), which mutation R5 specifically targets
Assuming a larger window size always helps without considering the proportional memory cost
follow_up_questions: What specific bug would mutation R5 (isSet addressing the wrong bit) cause, observably?
Why must the TOO_OLD check happen BEFORE the bitmap read, not after?
How would you change this indexing scheme if size needed to exceed 2^32 bits?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Using raw bit arithmetic (shift/mask) instead of a higher-level boolean array trades a little readability for a meaningful memory win (8x smaller than one byte per counter) -- for a per-session structure that exists for every active peer, this compounds at scale.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If the TOO_OLD guard were removed (mutation R2-style) while the slide-and-clear logic stayed, a sufficiently old counter would read whatever stale bit happens to occupy its slot now -- sometimes correctly TOO_OLD by luck, sometimes wrongly ACCEPT or REPLAY depending on what's currently in that slot, which is strictly worse than a deterministic answer.
advanced.alternatives: A growing Set<number> avoids bit-indexing complexity entirely but trades it for unbounded memory growth (see VPN-102) -- the bitmap's complexity is the direct cost of getting bounded memory.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x-100x sessions, each session's bitmap cost stays fixed regardless of traffic volume, which is exactly the point of this design -- the per-session memory does NOT grow with packet count, only with session COUNT.
advanced.production_improvements: Keep mutation tests (R1-R5) in CI permanently, since bit-indexing bugs are exactly the kind of subtle, hard-to-spot-by-inspection errors that regress silently without them.

question: Trace how VpnNode's real UDP socket 'message' event ends up dispatching a TRANSPORT_DATA packet to the correct Session.
answer_hinglish:
`VpnNode` constructor mein `this.socket.on('message', (data, rinfo) => this.handleMessage(data, {host, port}))` wired hota hai -- har UDP datagram seedha `handleMessage` tak pahunchta hai.

`handleMessage` pehle `peekMessageType(data)` se SIRF first byte read karta hai (bina poora decode kiye) -- agar `MessageType.TRANSPORT_DATA` (3) hai, `this.peer.decryptPacket(data)` call hota hai.

`Peer.decryptPacket` ab poora decode karta hai: `decodeTransportData(data)` se `{receiverId, counter, ciphertext, tag}` nikalta hai (MALFORMED throw nahi karta, catch karke typed reject deta hai). Phir `this.sessionsByReceiverId.get(fields.receiverId)` -- YEH hi exact dispatch step hai: receiverId se O(1) map lookup, koi socket address ya scan involved nahi. Agar entry nahi mili, `UNKNOWN_SESSION`.

Mila hua `entry.session.decrypt(counter, ciphertext, tag, aad)` call hota hai, jo anti-replay check + AEAD decrypt karta hai. Success par `{ok:true, peerName: entry.peerName, payload}` return hota hai. VpnNode isko `this.tun.deliver(result.payload)` se app ko deliver kar deta hai -- failure par `emitDropped()` se reason surface hota hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate network-event-to-business-logic dispatch chain ko accurately trace kar sakta hai, including WHERE exactly the receiver-id lookup happens.
real_world_analogy: Ek post office ek letter ka pin-code (receiverId) dekhta hai aur seedha correct sorting bin (session) mein daal deta hai -- woh letter ka sender address check karne ki zaroorat nahi, sirf addressed-to code.
how_it_works: socket 'message' event -> handleMessage -> peekMessageType routes by first byte -> Peer.decryptPacket decodes and looks up sessionsByReceiverId by fields.receiverId -> Session.decrypt does the actual anti-replay+AEAD work -> VpnNode.tun.deliver() on success.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts ke handleMessage method aur constructor ka socket.on('message', ...) wiring; src/peer.ts ka decryptPacket aur sessionsByReceiverId map.
advantages: Dispatch is a single map lookup, O(1) regardless of how many sessions exist
peekMessageType avoids fully decoding a message before knowing which decoder to even call
Never throws on malformed or unknown-session input -- always a typed rejection that VpnNode can log and move past
disadvantages: Any receiver-id collision across sessions would misdirect a packet (though ids are randomly generated per handshake)
The dispatch has no knowledge of which transport socket/address sent it -- by design, but means address spoofing cannot be caught at this layer
A single dgram socket handling all message types means one slow handler could, in principle, delay others (no per-type queueing)
common_mistakes: Assuming the socket address (rinfo) is used to find the session -- it is not, the receiverId is
Forgetting that peekMessageType only reads one byte and doesn't validate the rest of the message
Confusing decryptPacket's MALFORMED (bad wire format) with UNKNOWN_SESSION (well-formed but no matching session)
follow_up_questions: Why does dispatch use the receiverId instead of the socket address the packet arrived from?
What would happen if two different sessions somehow got the same receiverId?
How would you extend this dispatch to route to one of SEVERAL active remote peers (a concentrator)?

question: How does wire.ts construct the AAD (additional authenticated data) for each of the three message types, and why does each one bind different fields?
answer_hinglish:
AAD (Additional Authenticated Data) AEAD mein woh plaintext data hai jo encrypt nahi hoti par authentication tag mein bind hoti hai -- agar AAD change ho jaaye, decrypt fail hota hai, chahe ciphertext/tag khud untouched hon. Har message type ka AAD alag fields bind karta hai, jo us message ke context-specific tampering ko catch karta hai.

`handshakeInitAad(initiatorReceiverId, ephemeralPub)` = `uint32be(initiatorReceiverId) + ephemeralPub` -- yeh bind karta hai ki receiverId aur ephemeral key TAMPER na ho sakein bina decrypt fail kiye, chahe woh khud encrypted nahi hain (sirf static key ciphertext encrypted hai).

`handshakeResponseAad(responderReceiverId, initiatorReceiverId, ephemeralPub)` = teen fields ka concat -- yahan DONO receiverIds bind hote hain, taaki koi response ka receiverId swap na kar sake bina detection ke, plus responder ka ephemeral key.

`transportAad(receiverId, counter)` = `uint32be(receiverId) + uint64be(counter)` -- yeh TRANSPORT packets ke liye crucial hai: agar koi attacker sirf receiverId ya counter field change kare (par ciphertext/tag same rakhe), AEAD decrypt FAIL hoga, kyunki AAD mismatch ho jaayega. Yeh exactly woh property hai jo ensures karti hai ki ek packet 'relabeled' (different session ko bhej diya jaaye) nahi ja sakta without detection.
why_needed: Interviewer check karna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai AAD kyun zaroori hai -- plaintext metadata ko bhi tamper-proof banane ke liye, bina usey encrypt kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek sealed envelope ke BAAHAR likha address bhi ek tamper-evident seal se protected hai -- koi envelope ke andar ka letter nahi bhi padh sakta, par address change karne ki koshish bhi seal todegi.
how_it_works: Each *Aad function concatenates the specific header fields relevant to that message type into a Buffer passed as AEAD's AAD parameter; a mismatch in ANY bound field causes decrypt to throw, even if ciphertext and tag are otherwise valid.
in_this_project: src/wire.ts ke handshakeInitAad, handshakeResponseAad, transportAad functions; src/handshake.ts aur src/session.ts dono apne respective encrypt/decrypt calls mein yeh exact AAD pass karte hain.
advantages: Header fields are tamper-evident without needing to be encrypted themselves
Each message type binds exactly the fields relevant to its own tampering risks, no more no less
Mismatched AAD fails loudly via AEAD's own tag check -- no separate validation logic needed
disadvantages: Any change to a wire format field must be mirrored in its AAD construction, or the field becomes unprotected
AAD construction and wire encoding are two separate functions that must stay perfectly in sync by convention
Does not itself prevent a REPLAY of an untouched message -- that's AntiReplayWindow's separate job
common_mistakes: Forgetting to include a new header field in its AAD when extending the wire format
Assuming AAD mismatch and ciphertext tamper produce different error types -- both surface as the same AUTH_FAILED
