Is design mein woh technically harmless bhi hota (receiverIds alag hain, grace window sab packets bachata), par zero benefit ke liye double churn. Isliye PLAN.md ka decision: sirf woh side rekey karti hai jisne ORIGINALLY `initiateHandshake()` call kiya tha -- VpnNode mein woh hamesha woh node hai jisne `connect()` kiya.

Implementation: `PeerSessionState` mein ek `role` field hai ('initiator'/'responder'). `installSession()` usko `previous?.role ?? defaultRole` se set karta hai -- matlab role sirf PEHLE session par decide hota hai, aur har rekey use aage carry karta hai. `receiveHandshakeResponse` 'initiator' pass karta hai, `receiveHandshakeInit` 'responder', par yeh default sirf first time use hota hai.

Isliye agar responder (bob) khud manually `initiateHandshake('alice')` call kar de (Peer API isko rokta nahi), handshake succeed hoga, generation badhega, par bob ka role 'responder' hi rahega. `checkRekey()` mein pehla filter `if (state.role !== "initiator") continue;` hai, toh bob kabhi automatic rekey report nahi karega. Responder sirf respond karta hai -- ek naye HANDSHAKE_INIT ko waise hi handle karta hai jaise pehle karta tha.
why_needed: Distributed systems mein 'kaun action lega' ka ek single owner hona duplicate work aur race conditions se bachata hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate yeh ownership explicit kar sakta hai aur bata sakta hai ki woh state mein kahan record hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Do log phone par baat kar rahe hain aur line kharab ho jaaye -- agar dono ek saath call back karein toh dono ko busy tone milti hai. Pehle se tay hai ki jisne pehle call kiya tha wahi dobara call karega, doosra bas utha lega.
how_it_works: role is recorded once, at the first installSession for a peer name, and carried forward (previous?.role ?? defaultRole). checkRekey() skips every peer whose role is not 'initiator', so a responder-role session never appears in its result no matter how much time passes or how many messages it sends.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts: PeerSessionState.role, installSession (`role: previous?.role ?? defaultRole`), checkRekey (`if (state.role !== "initiator") continue;`). test/rekey.test.ts: 'a rekey triggers automatically once the configured time threshold is reached' (bob.checkRekey returns [] even with rekeyAfterMs set) aur 'the original RESPONDER manually re-handshaking does not make it eligible for automatic rekeying'. Mutations RK1 (role guard removed) aur RK12 (role not carried forward) dono caught.
advantages: No simultaneous double-rekey: exactly one side owns the decision
Matches VpnNode's existing single-dialer shape, so no new coordination protocol is needed
Configuring rekey options on both peers is harmless -- the responder simply never acts on them
disadvantages: If the initiator's process stops calling checkRekey (no timer started), the session never rekeys, even if the responder wanted it to
The responder's own sent-message count is never a trigger, so heavy responder-to-initiator traffic is only bounded by the initiator's triggers
common_mistakes: Recomputing role from whichever side started the latest handshake, so a manual re-handshake by the responder flips ownership (RK12)
Letting both sides run timers 'for robustness' and then debugging duplicate handshakes
Assuming the responder rejects a rekey HANDSHAKE_INIT -- it handles it exactly like the first one
follow_up_questions: What would break, if anything, if both sides were allowed to rekey independently in this design?
Should the responder be able to request a rekey, and how would you signal that without letting it initiate?
Why is a responder's heavy send volume not a rekey trigger here?

question: What happens if a rekey's HANDSHAKE_INIT is lost on the wire, and what is different if instead its HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE is lost?
answer_hinglish:
Lost HANDSHAKE_INIT (yeh tested case hai): initiator ne `initiateHandshake()` se ek pending entry banayi (`pendingHandshakes`, `startedAt` ke saath), par responder tak kuch nahi pahuncha. `installSession()` sirf successful receive par chalta hai, toh dono sides ka current session bilkul untouched hai -- traffic dono directions mein normal chalta rehta hai. Jab tak pending entry hai, `checkRekey()` us peer ko dobara report nahi karta. `rekeyRetryMs` (default 5000) ke baad `abandonStaleRekeyAttempts()` woh entry delete karta hai, aur agla `checkRekey()` fresh ephemeral keypair ke saath retry karta hai. Yeh sweep sirf un peers par lagta hai jinka session already hai -- first-ever `connect()` ka pending entry chhua nahi jaata, kyunki uska apna promise timeout hai (RK8).

Lost HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE: yeh subtle hai, aur code se trace karke nikalta hai -- test/rekey.test.ts mein iska test NAHI hai. Responder naya session tab install karta hai jab woh response BHEJTA hai, toh uska `current` ab naya session hai aur `encryptPacket()` naye session ke saath initiator ke NAYE receiverId par bhejta hai. Par initiator ke paas woh id sirf `pendingHandshakes` mein hai, `sessionsByReceiverId` mein nahi -- toh responder->initiator packets initiator par UNKNOWN_SESSION se drop honge jab tak retry succeed na ho. Initiator->responder direction bachi rehti hai: initiator purane session par bhejta hai, aur responder ka purana session `retiring` hai, `rekeyGraceMs` (10000) tak. Defaults mein retry (5000) grace se pehle aata hai, isliye woh direction sahi chalti hai -- par ek direction ka short outage real hai. PLAN.md ka 'lost handshake leaves current session untouched' initiator ki state ke baare mein sach hai, responder ki state ke baare mein nahi.
why_needed: UDP par koi bhi message lost ho sakta hai, aur rekey ek multi-message protocol hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate HAR message ke loss ko alag se trace kar sake, aur honestly bata sake ki kaunsa path tested hai aur kaunsa sirf code reading se pata hai.
real_world_analogy: Tum building manager ko naya lock lagane ki request bhejte ho. Agar request hi kho gayi, kuch nahi badla -- purani chaabi sab jagah chalti hai, tum thodi der baad dobara bhejte ho. Par agar manager ne lock badal diya aur 'yeh rahi nayi chaabi' wala letter kho gaya, toh manager ki taraf se aane wale log nayi chaabi use kar rahe hain jo tumhare paas nahi hai.
how_it_works: Lost INIT: nothing is installed anywhere; pending entry ages out after rekeyRetryMs via abandonStaleRekeyAttempts (only for peers with an established session), then checkRekey reports the peer again. Lost RESPONSE: receiveHandshakeInit already ran installSession on the responder (new current, old one retiring for rekeyGraceMs), while the initiator still has the old current and only a pending entry for the new receiverId.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts: initiateHandshake (pending entry with startedAt), receiveHandshakeInit (installs on send), abandonStaleRekeyAttempts (`this.peerSessions.has(pending.peerName) && now - pending.startedAt >= this.rekeyRetryMs`), checkRekey (skips peers with a pending attempt). test/rekey.test.ts: 'a lost rekey HANDSHAKE_INIT does not disrupt the still-valid old session, and a later rekey attempt succeeds' (rekeyRetryMs 500: 499ms -> [], 500ms -> due again) aur 'checkRekey does not abandon a pending FIRST handshake with no established session yet'. Lost-RESPONSE path ka koi test nahi hai.
advantages: A lost rekey INIT costs nothing but a delay: no session is touched and the retry is automatic
The retry sweep is scoped to rekeys only, so it never races VpnNode.connect()'s own timeout
Default rekeyRetryMs (5000) < rekeyGraceMs (10000), so the initiator-to-responder direction survives a lost response if the retry succeeds
disadvantages: A lost HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE causes a real responder-to-initiator outage until the retry completes (derived from code, untested)
Retry timing depends on how often checkRekey runs (VpnNode.startRekeyTimer default 1000ms), on top of rekeyRetryMs
No backoff: a peer that keeps losing handshakes is retried at a fixed cadence
common_mistakes: Tearing down or replacing the current session when a rekey starts, instead of when it completes
Letting the stale-attempt sweep also delete a first-handshake pending entry (the RK8 mutation)
Assuming 'the old session is untouched' holds for BOTH sides -- the responder switched the moment it sent its response
follow_up_questions: How would you write a test that reproduces the lost-HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE outage with two Peer objects and a ManualClock?
What change would let the responder keep sending on the old session until it sees the initiator use the new one?
Why must rekeyRetryMs be smaller than rekeyGraceMs, and what happens if it is not?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Installing on send keeps the handshake at two messages (Noise-IK shape) and makes the lost-INIT case trivially safe, but it means the responder can switch before the initiator knows. Real WireGuard handles this by having the responder not use the new keypair for sending until it receives the first data packet from the initiator under it (key confirmation); this project skipped that.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Lost INIT: zero impact, retry after rekeyRetryMs. Lost RESPONSE: responder-to-initiator packets dropped as UNKNOWN_SESSION until the retry lands; if rekeyRetryMs were configured above rekeyGraceMs, the initiator-to-responder direction would also break once the responder's retiring session expired. A late response arriving after its attempt was abandoned is rejected as NO_PENDING_HANDSHAKE and is harmless.
advanced.alternatives: Responder keeps sending on its old session until the first packet arrives on the new one (key confirmation); a third confirmation message; or exponential backoff on retries instead of a fixed rekeyRetryMs.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: With many peers on lossy links, lost responses become a steady background of short one-direction outages, and fixed-cadence retries from many initiators can synchronize; jitter and backoff matter more at scale.
advanced.production_improvements: Add the missing lost-response test, implement responder-side key confirmation before switching its send session, add jitter/backoff to rekey retries, and validate rekeyRetryMs < rekeyGraceMs at construction.

question: Why does every rekey start a brand-new anti-replay window and send counter, instead of carrying the old session's counter state forward?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki anti-replay window aur counter dono ek specific KEY ke saath bandhe hain, peer ke saath nahi. Nonce-reuse ka rule hai 'ek given key ke saath ek nonce kabhi do baar nahi'. Rekey ek naya handshake hai, naye ephemeral keys se naye sendKey/recvKey nikalte hain -- toh naye session mein counter 0 phir se use karna bilkul safe hai, kyunki (naya key, counter 0) pehle kabhi use hi nahi hua.

Is project mein yeh structurally guaranteed hai: har rekey `installSession()` se ek `new Session(...)` banata hai, aur Session ka constructor hamesha `sendCounter = 0` aur ek fresh `new AntiReplayWindow()` banata hai. Koi code path purane session ka counter ya bitmap copy nahi karta.

Agar carry forward karte toh ulta problem hota: purane window ka `highest` maan lo 10,000 hai, aur naya sender 0 se shuru karta hai -- naye session ka har packet TOO_OLD ya REPLAY reject ho jaata. Aur security kuch nahi badhti: ek purane session ka captured packet naye session ke against kaam hi nahi karta -- woh purane receiverId par addressed hai (retiring session tak jaata hai, jiska apna window usse REPLAY pakadta hai, ya grace ke baad UNKNOWN_SESSION), aur agar koi receiverId badal bhi de, toh AAD aur key dono badal gaye hain, AEAD tag fail hoga.

Test mein yeh directly dikhaya hai: same wire counter 0 purane session par ek baar aur naye par ek baar accept hota hai, aur har window apna exact replay alag se reject karta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer check karta hai ki tum samajhte ho ki nonce aur replay state per-KEY hoti hai -- yeh TLS, SSH, WireGuard sab mein same idea hai, aur rekey ke time log galti se 'counter continue karo' soch lete hain.
real_world_analogy: Har naye cheque book ke cheque number 1 se shuru hote hain -- bank confuse nahi hota kyunki account/book alag hai. Purani book ka 'last used number' nayi book par lagana sab naye cheques reject kara deta.
how_it_works: Session fields are initialised per instance: private sendCounter = 0; private readonly window = new AntiReplayWindow(). installSession always constructs a new Session, so the new generation's counter space and replay bitmap start empty, independent of the retiring session, which keeps its own window until it is pruned.
in_this_project: src/session.ts ka Session class (sendCounter aur window field initialisers); src/peer.ts ka installSession (`new Session(sendKey, recvKey, myReceiverId, peerReceiverId)`). test/rekey.test.ts: 'the old and new sessions' anti-replay windows are independent (same counter value accepted on each)'. PLAN.md 'Stage 2 decisions' point 5.
advantages: Correct by construction: no code path can accidentally share counter or bitmap state across keys
Each rekey also resets the counter far away from the 2^53 precision limit
Old and new sessions can both accept packets during the grace window without interfering
disadvantages: Two windows are alive during the grace period (2 x 256 bytes per peer) -- trivial, but real
common_mistakes: Carrying the old highest counter into the new session, so every new packet is rejected as TOO_OLD
Thinking counter 0 reuse after a rekey is nonce reuse -- the key changed, so the (key, nonce) pair is new
Assuming an old captured packet could be replayed into the new session -- different receiverId, AAD and key
follow_up_questions: What exactly would break if the sender kept counting from its old value but the receiver started a fresh window?
Why is nonce uniqueness defined per key rather than per peer?

question: Why does Peer.checkRekey() take an optional `now` and use an injected Clock instead of starting its own setInterval, and how do the tests use that?
answer_hinglish:
Stage 1 mein is project ko time ka koi concept hi nahi chahiye tha. Stage 2 ke rekey triggers time par depend karte hain, toh `src/clock.ts` aaya -- `Clock` interface (`now(): number`), real use ke liye `systemClock` (`Date.now()`), aur tests ke liye `ManualClock` (`set`, `advance`). Yeh exactly wahi shape hai jo repo ke doosre projects (22-messaging, 23-password-manager, 25-dns-sinkhole) already use karte hain.

Design rule hai 'driver inject karo, chupao mat': Peer khud koi timer start nahi karta. `checkRekey(now = this.clock.now())` ek pure read hai local state ka, plus do chhoti cleanup sweeps (`pruneRetiredSessions`, `abandonStaleRekeyAttempts`), aur sirf ek list return karta hai ki kaunse peers due hain -- `{peerName, reason}`. Actually handshake bhejna caller ka kaam hai. `VpnNode.checkRekey()` us list par `initiateHandshake()` call karke UDP par bhejta hai, aur `VpnNode.startRekeyTimer(intervalMs = 1000)` hi woh jagah hai jahan real `setInterval` rehta hai (`stopRekeyTimer` aur `close()` usko clear karte hain).

Fayda tests mein dikhta hai: test `ManualClock(0)` banata hai, `clock.advance(999)` karke assert karta hai ki `checkRekey()` `[]` deta hai, phir `advance(1)` karke `[{peerName: 'bob', reason: 'TIME'}]`. Koi sleep nahi, koi flakiness nahi, aur boundary exactly test hoti hai -- isliye RK3 (time boundary off by one) jaise mutations pakde gaye. Agar Peer ke andar setInterval hota, har test ko real time wait karna padta aur exact boundary test karna lagbhag impossible hota.
why_needed: Time-dependent code ko testable banana ek common interview topic hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki tum clock injection aur 'decision vs. driver' separation samajhte ho, aur exact boundary tests kaise likhte ho.
real_world_analogy: Ek alarm system jo khud ghadi nahi rakhta, balki diwar ki ghadi se time poochta hai -- testing ke time tum diwar ki ghadi ko haath se aage kar sakte ho aur turant dekh sakte ho ki alarm bajta hai ya nahi, raat bhar intezaar kiye bina.
how_it_works: Peer stores options.clock ?? systemClock. initiateHandshake records startedAt = clock.now(); installSession records establishedAt and retireAt from clock.now(); checkRekey(now) compares against those. VpnNode.checkRekey(now?) forwards to Peer.checkRekey and sends a HANDSHAKE_INIT for each due peer; startRekeyTimer wraps it in setInterval.
in_this_project: src/clock.ts: Clock, systemClock, ManualClock (advance() negative ya non-finite ms par RangeError deta hai). src/peer.ts: PeerOptions.clock, checkRekey(now). src/transport.ts: VpnNode.checkRekey, startRekeyTimer, stopRekeyTimer, close. test/rekey.test.ts: 'a rekey is NOT due before the configured time threshold is reached' (advance 999), 'stopRekeyTimer actually stops the periodic rekey check from firing again', 'close() stops any running rekey timer so it never fires into an already-closed socket'. Mutations TK3/TK4 timer lifecycle ke liye caught.
advantages: Exact boundary tests (999 vs 1000 ms) with no sleeping and no flakiness
Peer stays a pure, socket-free state machine, consistent with stage 1's design
The timer lives in one place (VpnNode) with an explicit stop path, so it cannot leak past close()
disadvantages: Forgetting to call checkRekey (or startRekeyTimer) silently disables rekeying
Rekey timing granularity is the timer interval: a session can run up to intervalMs past its threshold
common_mistakes: Calling Date.now() directly inside protocol logic, making boundary tests depend on real time
Starting a setInterval in a constructor with no way to stop it, leaking timers in tests
Not clearing the interval in close(), so a tick fires into a closed socket (the TK4 mutation)
follow_up_questions: Why does startRekeyTimer call stopRekeyTimer first?
How would you test the real-timer path without making the test slow or flaky?
What is the worst-case delay between a session crossing rekeyAfterMs and the rekey HANDSHAKE_INIT going out?
